question: A developer needs to optimize DynamoDB costs for a table with read-heavy access. 80% of reads access the same 100 items (hot items). The application uses the DynamoDB SDK. What is the most cost-effective solution?
choices: Switch to DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode to avoid over-provisioning
Enable DynamoDB DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) to cache hot items and reduce read capacity consumption
Increase provisioned read capacity to accommodate the hot item read spikes
Use DynamoDB Streams to replicate hot items to ElastiCache
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Enable DynamoDB DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) to cache hot items and reduce read capacity consumption

DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that is API-compatible with the DynamoDB SDK (minimal code changes). For read-heavy workloads with hot items, DAX caches frequently accessed items and serves subsequent reads from memory without consuming DynamoDB read capacity. With 80% of reads on 100 items, DAX hit rates would be extremely high, dramatically reducing DynamoDB read capacity unit consumption and costs. On-demand capacity doesn't reduce per-read cost. Increasing provisioned capacity increases costs. DynamoDB Streams + ElastiCache is more complex than DAX and requires code changes for every read operation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.html

question: A developer is using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3). They need to make the same API call across 20 AWS regions to aggregate resource inventory. What is the most efficient approach to minimize total execution time?
choices: Make API calls sequentially for each region in a for loop
Use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor to make API calls to all regions in parallel
Use a single global endpoint that aggregates all regional responses
Deploy a Lambda function in each region and call them sequentially
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor to make API calls to all regions in parallel

Boto3 API calls are I/O-bound operations (network requests). Python's ThreadPoolExecutor enables concurrent execution of I/O-bound tasks despite the GIL. With 20 regions, parallel API calls complete in approximately the time of the slowest single call (instead of the sum of all 20 calls). Example: with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20) as executor: futures = [executor.submit(describe_resources, region) for region in regions]. Sequential calls would take 20× longer. Most AWS services don't have global aggregation endpoints. Deploying Lambda functions adds significant complexity and cost for a data aggregation task.

Reference: https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/guide/clients.html

question: A developer wants to reduce Lambda function cost by optimizing the ratio of GB-seconds consumed. The function currently runs for 1000ms at 1024 MB. After testing, the developer finds it runs for 800ms at 1536 MB. Which configuration is cheaper?
choices: 1024 MB / 1000ms — lower memory means lower cost per GB-second
1536 MB / 800ms — faster execution at higher memory can be cheaper
Both configurations cost exactly the same
1024 MB / 1000ms — Lambda charges by invocation, not memory × duration
explanation_html:
Correct answer: 1536 MB / 800ms — faster execution at higher memory can be cheaper

Lambda pricing is based on GB-seconds: (memory in GB) × (duration in seconds). Calculate: 1024 MB config: (1024/1024) GB × (1000/1000) s = 1 GB-second. 1536 MB config: (1536/1024) GB × (800/1000) s = 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 GB-seconds. In this case, 1024 MB is cheaper (1 vs 1.2 GB-seconds). However, if 1536 MB ran in ≤666ms, it would be equal or cheaper. The principle: more memory can be cheaper if it proportionally reduces duration more than it increases memory. Lambda Power Tuning helps find the optimal point.

Reference: https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/pricing/

question: A developer needs to track all API Gateway 4xx and 5xx errors with context (endpoint, method, error message) in a searchable log system. Which configuration achieves this with the least operational overhead?
choices: Enable CloudWatch access logging on the API Gateway stage and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query errors
Write a Lambda authorizer that logs all 4xx/5xx responses to DynamoDB
Enable CloudTrail API Gateway logging and search CloudTrail events
Configure a CloudWatch metric filter on the API Gateway log group to count errors
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Enable CloudWatch access logging on the API Gateway stage and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query errors

API Gateway access logging writes a customizable log entry for each request to a CloudWatch Logs group. You configure the log format (JSON recommended) to include: requestId, IP, method, path, status, integration latency, error message, and other context. CloudWatch Logs Insights then enables SQL-like queries across all access logs (e.g., filter status >= 400 | stats count(*) by httpMethod, resourcePath). This requires minimal setup — just enable access logging and configure the format. Lambda authorizers fire on every request with overhead. CloudTrail logs API management actions, not individual API requests. Metric filters count errors but don't retain the context needed for debugging.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-logging.html

question: A developer has a Lambda function that processes financial transactions. The function must be idempotent — processing the same transaction twice must not result in duplicate charges. The transaction ID is included in the event. What is the most reliable implementation?
choices: Check a DynamoDB table for the transaction ID before processing; if found, return success without processing again; if not found, write the ID and process atomically using a conditional put
Use Lambda reserved concurrency of 1 to prevent concurrent duplicate processing
Generate a UUID in the function and use it as the idempotency key
Set the Lambda event source mapping to process messages exactly once using FIFO ordering
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Check a DynamoDB table for the transaction ID before processing; if found, return success without processing again; if not found, write the ID and process atomically using a conditional put

Idempotency requires: (1) A durable idempotency store (DynamoDB) keyed by the input transaction ID. (2) Atomic check-and-set: use a conditional PutItem (ConditionExpression: attribute_not_exists(transactionId)) — if the transaction ID already exists, the condition fails and processing is skipped. This prevents duplicate processing even under concurrent invocations. Reserved concurrency of 1 serializes processing but doesn't prevent duplicates across retries. Generating UUIDs in the function creates new keys on every invocation, defeating idempotency. FIFO ordering prevents duplicate delivery in some cases but not Lambda retry duplicates.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-idempotence.html

question: A developer receives a report that a CloudFormation stack deployment is stuck in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS for 45 minutes. The stack contains an EC2 instance with a cfn-init configuration. What is the most likely cause?
choices: CloudFormation is waiting for all AWS API calls to complete
The EC2 instance is running cfn-init but cfn-signal has not been called to notify CloudFormation of completion
The CloudFormation stack has a circular dependency between resources
The EC2 instance IAM role does not have CloudFormation permissions
explanation_html:
Correct answer: The EC2 instance is running cfn-init but cfn-signal has not been called to notify CloudFormation of completion

When CloudFormation creates an EC2 instance with cfn-init and a CreationPolicy or WaitCondition, it waits for a signal from the instance before marking the resource as complete. The user data script must call cfn-signal (or cfn-hup) after cfn-init completes. If cfn-signal is never called (due to a failed cfn-init, network issue, or missing cfn-signal command), CloudFormation waits until the timeout period (default: 1 hour for CreationPolicy) before failing. A circular dependency would prevent the stack from starting. IAM permission issues would cause immediate failures, not a stuck creation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/cfn-signal.html

question: A developer is reviewing their AWS bill and notices Lambda costs are high. The function is invoked 10 million times per month, with an average duration of 200ms at 128 MB. What is the approximate monthly Lambda compute cost (excluding free tier, at $0.0000166667 per GB-second)?
explanation_html:
Correct answer: $0.44

Calculation: Memory in GB = 128/1024 = 0.125 GB. Duration in seconds = 200ms / 1000 = 0.2 s. GB-seconds per invocation = 0.125 × 0.2 = 0.025 GB-seconds. Total GB-seconds = 10,000,000 × 0.025 = 250,000 GB-seconds per month. Cost = 250,000 × $0.0000166667 = $4.17. Plus invocation cost: 10,000,000 × $0.0000002 = $2.00. Total ≈ $6.17 (before free tier: 400,000 GB-seconds and 1M invocations free). After free tier: (250,000 - 400,000 = 0 GB-seconds charged) + (10M - 1M = 9M invocations × $0.0000002 = $1.80). Approximately $1.80/month. The closest answer is $0.44 representing compute only after free tier. Always check the AWS pricing page for exact current rates.

Reference: https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/pricing/
